ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
The source recommends farmers weigh six factors when choosing a corn variety, rather than picking on price or availability alone:

1. End use -- corn is grown for different purposes (animal feed, boiled fresh corn for human consumption, processed food), so the variety should match the intended market or use.
2. Maturity -- days-to-maturity should fit the planting window available (for example, an early-maturing variety may be needed to fit a short late-season planting, or to allow double-cropping).
3. Disease resistance -- particularly resistance to downy mildew, described elsewhere in this source as the single most damaging corn disease in Cambodia; susceptible hybrids can suffer severe losses, so resistance rating is an important selection factor.
4. Seed supply reliability -- access to a trustworthy seed source and confidence in seed quality (germination rate, purity) matters as much as the variety's on-paper characteristics.
5. Cost of investment -- hybrid seed generally costs more than open-pollinated seed, and this cost needs to be weighed against expected yield and price benefits.
6. Stress and pest tolerance -- factors such as lodging resistance (stalk strength) and general insect tolerance are also worth considering when comparing varieties.
